title: A right of first refusal lapses silently after four weeks, reverting the opportunity by default
content:
A.2.8.2.1.2.4.1 sets the mechanics: on written notification of a new DeFi opportunity, "Spark has four weeks to decide whether it wants to deploy SparkLend or lend to the target chain and protocol. If Spark opts not to do so by the end of the four-week period, Grove is permitted to pursue the opportunity" — subject to Grove's own security and risk assessments. The worked example is explicit that inaction suffices: "if Spark does not issue a formal refusal, the opportunity reverts to Grove after four weeks."

Default-to-lapse is the right choice for an option over a time-sensitive asset. A first-mover advantage in a new protocol deployment decays quickly, so a ROFR requiring affirmative release would let the holder freeze an opportunity indefinitely by simply not responding — converting a preference right into a veto.

The four-week window is a real commitment on both sides. It is long enough for genuine diligence on a new chain and protocol, and short enough that the opportunity usually survives it. Grove pays for the exclusivity carve-out it received by absorbing that delay on everything new.

This is the same silence-is-consent construction the Atlas uses in monthly settlement, where an undisputed figure becomes an Agreed Amount after five days. In both cases the burden of acting falls on the party who wants to change the default, and the process cannot be stalled by non-response.

A.2.8.2.1.2.4.2 adds a third path the binary framing would miss: for a "large enough cross-chain opportunity" the parties may combine — "Grove may deploy stablecoin liquidity on a target chain and Spark may deploy a SparkLend instance" — so the ROFR sets a fallback, not a prohibition on cooperating.
description: Spark has four weeks from Grove's written notification to decide on a cross-chain opportunity; no formal refusal is needed, since expiry of the window has the same effect as declining.
